newsitem.title: UK: UK pension funds missing performance goals - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK pension funds missing performance goals - survey.

text.p: British pension fund managers are increasingly failing to meet their investment performance targets, according to a new study by consultants WM Company.
Over the past three years only seven percent of funds outperformed the average by more than two percent, according to the survey, which covered over 1,500 funds worth more than 400 billion stg.

"Investment managers are often set targets of beating the average pension fund performance by one or two percent a year but WM's research shows this usually ensures a high rate of disappointment, given the expectations raised," said Gordon Bagot, of WM Company.

The ability of active fund managers to meet investment objectives and justify their higher fees has come under scrutiny in recent weeks, following a critical report from Britain's Office for Fair Trading (OFT).

In July OFT director general John Bridgeman called for a move to so-called "tracker funds", saying there was "no convincing evidence that fund managers can consistently outperform the market over the period of a pension plan".
Ten years ago nearly 15 percent of fund managers were able to beat the average by more than two percent over three years, according to the study.
"In that time, fund portfolios have remained just as diversified among asset classes but the range of returns from the different classes has narrowed," Bagot said.
So with asset classes performing relatively similarly, fund managers had a harder time beating the pack by picking a winning asset class, Bagot said.
"As a result, the targets have become more difficult to meet and other research shows that the fund which achieve them are unlikely to continue doing so in succeeding years."
WM Company also looked specifically at the group of funds which had been set one percent or two percent outperformance targets between 1992 and 1996.
These fund had relatively good success initially but performance declined steeply over time.
In 1992 almost half the funds with a target of beating the average by one percent were successful but the proportion succeeding fell to 21 percent in 1996.

"These results confirm out analysis in previous research which suggests that performance consistency is very hard to achieve," Bagot said. "They also confirm our previous findings that managers are often selected following strong recent performance but fail to sustain it."
